# Named Technical Account Manager

`customer_support.model.named_tam` · model · parent `—`

> One named human owns an account's entire support relationship. The customer has a person, not a queue: they mail them directly, they have their mobile number, and they stop re-explaining their environment because the person on the other end already knows it. That is the product, and it is genuinely valuable — the cost of re-establishing context is the largest invisible tax in pooled support, and this model deletes it. . It deletes it by concentrating it. Everything the TAM knows is in one head and almost none of it is in the ticket, because writing it down has no local benefit to the only person who reads the ticket. Leave, illness and resignation are therefore not staffing events, they are outages, and they are outages the dashboard cannot show. The handoff of a TAM account is the highest-risk operation in this branch and it is a relationship event before it is a records event: the successor inherits the tickets and none of the standing. . The second structural fact is that the service level actually delivered drifts far above the service level sold. A contract carries a four-hour first response; a TAM who likes the customer answers in nine minutes for a year. Nothing was renegotiated, but the customer's expectation now sits at nine minutes, and the first four-hour response — which is compliant — reads as abandonment and produces an escalation about a contract we did not breach. This is why entitlement is emphasised in a branch where nobody ever checks it: the gap between entitlement and habit is the branch's characteristic complaint. . Third: work arrives out of band. Direct mail, a shared Slack channel, a phone call on the way to something else. That work is real, consumes the TAM's day, and is invisible to every operational instrument the company owns, so cost-to-serve on a TAM account is systematically understated and the model always looks cheaper than it is. . What an operator carries over wrongly from a pooled queue: capacity intuition. In a pool the marginal ticket is absorbed by whoever is free, and adding an account degrades service at the margin. Here the marginal account is added to a specific person's book and degrades every account in that book simultaneously, because the resource being divided is one human's attention and their memory of eleven environments. Portfolio size is the only real lever in this branch, and it is usually set by a sales forecast rather than by anyone who has run one.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | a small named set of technical contacts per account, known personally, who route around any process that is slower than mailing the TAM |
| typical_resolution_hours | 6 |
| typical_acv | high — a named TAM is either a premium SKU or an unpriced concession made during a renewal, and which of the two it is decides whether it can ever be withdrawn |
| volume_shape | low ticket count, high touch count; volume tracks the account's own project calendar — upgrades, migrations, audits — not the product's release cycle |
| staffing_model | one named technical account manager per account or small portfolio, with a backline of specialists they pull in by name rather than by queue |
| coverage | the TAM's working hours, plus an informal willingness to answer outside them that is not a coverage model and cannot be rostered |
| automation_level | very low, and deliberately so — a named contact who is sent a help-centre link reads it as being handed back to the queue they paid to leave |
| primary_channels | `email`, `phone`, `chat`, `ticket_portal` |
| notes | The failure this branch is most often killed by is not cost, it is concentration. One TAM leaving takes three accounts' worth of unwritten context with them, and the resulting churn is booked against the accounts rather than against the model. Anything that forces context into the record — even a thin handoff note — is worth more here than in any other branch, and is exactly what nobody does because the person who would benefit does not exist yet.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement`

Requires `has_technical_account_manager`, `named_contacts`, `named_contact_limit`, `plan`


> The named contact list is the branch's only enforceable boundary and the one nobody enforces. A TAM answers whoever mails them, the list drifts from four people to nineteen over a term, and the account is then receiving a service several times what was sold — which is invisible until renewal, when withdrawing it is impossible without a fight. `has_technical_account_manager` matters because it distinguishes a TAM that was bought from a TAM that was conceded, and only the first can be repriced.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.requester`

Requires `is_named_contact`, `role_title`, `vip_flag`


> In a pooled branch these are useful; here they are the routing table. The relationship is with specific humans, so a new name appearing on a thread is a material event — it is either the account expanding beyond what was sold or, more often, the beginning of a personnel change that will cost the TAM their standing.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `assignee_ref`, `agent_touch_count`


> The assignee carries almost no information in this branch — it is the same person on everything — so the attribute that means something is how many OTHER people have touched the ticket. Zero is normal. A rising number means the TAM is out, overloaded, or has hit the edge of what they can hold, and it is the earliest available reading of the model's real failure mode.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.commitment`

Requires `origin_channel`, `wording_verbatim`, `made_by_ref`


> A promise made by a named person is personal in a way a queue's promise is not, and it is kept at a higher rate and remembered far longer when broken. It is also usually made in a channel that keeps no record. The commitment object is the mechanism by which anything said on a phone call survives the call; without it this branch's promises exist only in the customer's notes, and they will be quoted from those notes.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.escalation`

Requires `receiving_owner_ref`, `reason`


> There is no ladder above a TAM — escalation goes sideways to engineering or upward to an executive, and either way it routes around the named owner. The customer understands exactly what they are doing when they do it, which is why an escalation on a TAM account is a statement about the relationship and not only about the ticket. Treat a first-ever escalation from a named contact as a higher-severity signal than a fifth escalation from a pooled account.
